>> This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign has filed a lawsuit
against Alaska election officials seeking records
on rejected absentee ballots.
The campaign wants to know whose ballots were rejected and why,
saying that information is needed
to ensure lawful votes are counted.
Peltola, a Democrat, holds a narrow lead
over Republican Senator Dan Sullivan
in a race still too close to call.
In a message to supporters, Peltola urged patience.
>> We are being patient,
waiting for more ballots to come in in Alaska.
It just takes a little bit longer
as we wait for all of the ballots to come in.
We know that tens of thousands of ballots
still need to be counted,
and those are going to be early in-person ballots
and absentee ballots.
>> State officials say the records are preliminary
and releasing them now could delay the count.
A new report offering the latest look at inflation
is due out this week.
Frustration over the cost of living
helped drive Republican losses in the midterms,
and PR Stephen Bisahop reports strong economic growth
hasn't eased the pressure on American budgets.
The week before the election,
we got an economic split-screen look at the country
from the Commerce Department.
The first broadest view of the economy showed it doing well.
Gross domestic product for the U.S. grew
at an annual rate of 3.4% over the summer.
That's a strong pace of growth,
driven by investment in AI and consumer spending.
But American voters were paying much more attention
to the other screen.
It showed inflation in September up 3.6% from a year earlier.
Americans are still spending but getting less for it.
Higher energy costs are driving inflation.
That is directly due to the U.S. war against Iran
launched by President Trump
and led to Americans punishing Republicans
Tuesday with their votes.
Stephen Bisahop, NPR News.
>> Poland has begun two days of mourning
after a gumming killed at least six people
and wounded more than a dozen others in Krakow.
NPR's Esme Nicholson reports the suspect was shot
and arrested by police.
>> Police say the suspect, a Polish citizen in his mid-20s,
drove into the heart of Krakow's old town,
a popular tourist destination,
and opened fire from his car, shooting people at random.
Searches are ongoing at the suspect's home,
where authorities found three dead bodies
they have now identified as the gunman's mother,
father, and 21-year-old sister.
Speaking to journalists,
Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kievinski says
the suspect holds very radical and ultra-nationalistic views.
Kievinski praised the heroism of police officers
for preventing what could have been a much larger massacre.
He said the officers, some of whom are seriously injured,
fired shots at the attacker just three minutes
after receiving reports.
For "NPR News," I'm Esme Nicholson in Berlin.
>> This is "NPR News" in Washington.
More than 600,000 electricity customers are without power
in central Ukraine today following Russian attacks.
Utility officials say key energy facilities were damaged.
Hospitals and other critical services
have switched to backup generators.
Crews are working to restore electricity
with essential facilities getting priority.
A strong earthquake hit central Japan early today,
injuring at least 22 people.
NPR's Anthony Kuhn reports authorities are warning
of strong aftershocks in the coming days.
>> The quake hit just after 1 a.m. local time
and was centered on central Shizuoka Prefecture
at a depth of 25 miles below the Earth's surface.
>> Japan's meteorological agency put it at magnitude 5.7,
the U.S. Geological Survey at 5.5.
The quake threw some of the injured off stairs
or from their beds.
It shattered windows and sent merchandise
tumbling from store shelves.
Authorities reported that following the quake,
no changes were detected in the Nankai trough,
a fault line running along Japan's east coast.
Authorities put the chance of a magnitude 8 or 9 quake
centered on the trough at up to 50 to 90 percent
depending on the model in the next 30 years.
In a worst-case scenario,
that could cause up to 298,000 deaths.
Anthony Kuhn, NPR News, Seoul.
>> Pope Leo is wrapping up his three-day visit
to Uruguay today.
The pontiff has urged greater cooperation
between the church and government to help the poor.
He's scheduled to fly to Buenos Aires this afternoon
to begin the Argentina leg of his South American trip.
This is NPR News in Washington.
